newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jordan's king takes on Hebron challenge.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's king takes on Hebron challenge.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein, trying to salvage Israel-PLO negotiations over the West Bank town of Hebron, planned to meet Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday following talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

Jordanian Information Minister Marwan Muasher said the king would fly by helicopter from Gaza to Tel Aviv to see Netanyahu. King Hussein has been to Israel several times since signing a peace treaty with the Jewish state in 1994.
Netanyahu's office said he would meet the monarch at 2000 GMT.
Earlier, King Hussein travelled to Palestinian self-ruled Gaza after the United States said that its Middle East envoy would leave the region on Sunday night.

Envoy Dennis Ross arrived three weeks ago to try again to forge a deal to launch Palestinian self-rule in 80 percent of Hebron, a flashpoint of Arab-Israeli violence. The talks have hit an impasse over a timetable for Israeli troop withdrawals in rural areas of the West Bank following a Hebron pullback.

"He feels that the mediation role has been achieved, the assignment is complete," U.S. embassy spokesman Richard Scorza said. Asked if Ross's mission had failed for lack of an agreement, he said: "It's up to the parties to make the deal."
But later, a U.S. official described the situation as "fluid" and said it was not clear whether Ross would depart as planned.
"The (Arafat-King Hussein) meeting was very successful," Muasher told reporters.
"We had several contacts with Egyptian President (Hosni) Mubarak, (U.S. Secretary of State Warren) Christopher, Ross and Mr Netanyahu," he said.

"These efforts are a continuation of the Egyptian efforts to achieve a breakthrough, and the result of all these contacts is that his majesty will pay a visit to Tel Aviv to meet Mr Netanyahu," he said.
Palestinian Planning Minister Nabil Shaath said King Hussein's "personal influence" on Israel might help sway Netanyahu towards a Hebron deal.

Arafat's cabinet has accused Israel of violating its 1995 interim peace deal with the Palestine Liberation Organisation by demanding that future West Bank withdrawals, due to be completed by September 1997, be put off until May 1999.
Palestinians have rejected a U.S. compromise proposal that Israel complete further West Bank withdrawals by 1998.

King Hussein, Israel's closest Arab ally in the months following his 1994 peace treaty with the Jewish state, has distanced himself from Netanyahu over policies that include support for Jewish settlement expansion.

Israel was due to have completed the Hebron handover 10 months ago. But violence, security concerns, and other issues have held up a deal. Some 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs live in the town, holy to both as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.

King Hussein landed at Arafat's office in Gaza City after Israel refused a Palestinian request to receive the monarch's helicopter at an airport in the south of the strip. Israel demands security control of the airport.
King Hussein and Arafat have a history of uneasy relations, but Arab frustration with Netanyahu appears to have brought them closer together.
